title: Holy, holy, holy
hook: Orthodox churches sing Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us

segments.voice: Yesterday: the spiritual, songs of Moses and Jordan made by people who were not free. Your line was let my people go. Which song did you listen to? Day one hundred thirty-eight.

Sunday morning in an Orthodox church. Candles, icons, incense hanging in the air, and often no pews, just people standing. At a certain point in the service, the choir begins a short chant, and the whole church seems to lean into it. Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us. Then again. And again. Three times, sometimes more, slow enough that the words have room. It's short enough to learn on the way home. Today's word is its name, and its roots go back to a vision a prophet had in the Temple.
screen: `CANDLES, ICONS, INCENSE.` → `HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.` → `THREE TIMES, SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Trisagion. Greek: tris, three times, and hagion, holy. The thrice-holy. Its roots go back to the prophet Isaiah. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, and creatures called seraphim calling to one another. The King James Bible gives their words: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Why three times? Some readers hear Hebrew emphasis in it: say a word twice and it grows stronger; say it three times and there is nothing left to add. Holy beyond everything. At the end of the Bible, in Revelation, the song is still going: creatures around the throne "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." The Trisagion takes that cry and turns it into three lines people can pray: Holy God. Holy Mighty. Holy Immortal. And then one very human request: have mercy on us. Nobody knows for certain who first put it together. There's a story people tell, from Constantinople in the fifth century, of an earthquake, and a boy caught up into the sky who heard angels singing it. What the records do show is bishops crying it out at the Council of Chalcedon, in 451. In Orthodox churches it is sung at the Divine Liturgy, and Orthodox prayer books open the daily prayers with it. Catholics sing it too, in Greek and Latin, on Good Friday. In other churches, Christians sing Isaiah's three holies in the communion service, the Sanctus, and in a nineteenth-century hymn that begins the same way. The pattern holds in all of them: first praise beyond words, then a plea for mercy, close to the ground.
screen: `TRIS, HAGION — THRICE HOLY.` · `ISAIAH SEES THE SERAPHIM.` · `THREE TIMES: HOLY BEYOND ALL.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN MERCY.` · then, large: `HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit or stand, whichever you like; in Orthodox churches, people often stand to pray. Breathe in, and out. If you pray, you can say the Trisagion three times, slowly, one line per breath. Holy God. Holy Mighty. Holy Immortal. Have mercy on us. If you don't pray, you can simply say the words as words, and notice the shape: something vast, and then something small asking for mercy. After the third time, let the silence hold. The bell holds the time.
Trisagion. The thrice-holy. An ancient chant from Isaiah's vision: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.
Your line: close to the ground. Today, when something stops you in your tracks, a sky, a face, a piece of music, let those three words come. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians sing the Trisagion in the Divine Liturgy and pray it three times at the start of daily prayers, often making the sign of the cross each time; Catholics sing it on Good Friday, and many churches sing Isaiah's 'Holy, holy, holy' at communion.

original.note: Greek: thrice-holy, from tris, three times, and hagion, holy.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy, holy, holy is a hymn title.
what it means: the angels' cry in Isaiah, turned into a short chant: holy God, holy mighty, holy immortal, have mercy on us.
what a scholar hears: the Trisagion is attested at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. the triple holy is often read as Hebrew emphasis: holy beyond all.

notes: The Trisagion's English wording ('Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us') is the common Orthodox rendering; spoken but not listed as a quotation from a specific translation. Confirm wording.
Attested at the Council of Chalcedon (451): the acts record the bishops chanting it. Confirm.
The story of the boy caught up in the air during an earthquake in Constantinople (under Patriarch Proclus, 5th century) is presented as 'a story people tell'. Confirm.
Catholic use: sung in the Good Friday Reproaches (Improperia) in Greek and Latin (Hagios o Theos / Sanctus Deus). Confirm.
Hebrew repetition as superlative: standard explanation; confirm phrasing.
Reginald Heber's hymn Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty (published 1826) referred to as 'nineteenth-century hymn'. Confirm.
Tomorrow's title contains 'Taizé' with an accent; confirm the close screen renders it.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Walk into'; cut 'very likely no pews' and 'before most of Europe's cathedrals were built'. The Hebrew triple-holy as superlative ('as strong as it gets') is now 'some readers hear Hebrew emphasis'; 'fiery' (an etymology) cut; 'nearly every service' and 'every Sunday' cut. The 451 date now names its source (Acts of Chalcedon, added). The myth about the Hebrew superlative is replaced with the Trisagion's closing plea.
